svg.text: What a cryptographically relevant quantum computer would break · verified 14 Oct 2026, TLS measured live · snapshot 25 Oct 2026, 18:32 UTC

g.text: Install hashWhat hash does the default client check or pin a download against?
Publisher signatureWhat signs the artifact on the publisher's side?
Registry signatureWhat does the registry or its log sign artifacts or checkpoints with?
Transparency logWhat makes the log's history tamper-evident, and what signs its checkpoints?
Transport (TLS)Which TLS key exchange do the install and publish hosts negotiate? Server certificates are classical everywhere.
Publish credentialWhat authenticates an upload, and can a CRQC forge it from public data?
MFAWhich second factors does the registry offer?

rect.title: PyPI · Install hash: SHA-256 (PQ-safe). pip checks each file against the index's sha256.

PyPI · Publisher signature: ECDSA P-256 (quantum-vulnerable). Optional PEP 740 attestations. Sigstore bundle: ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key, certified by Fulcio's ECDSA P-384 CA. A CRQC could forge the CA and mint certificates for any identity. A post-quantum (ML-DSA) Sigstore instance is targeted for mid-2027 as a separate, opt-in trust root.
PyPI · Registry signature: none (not used). PyPI signs nothing (PEP 458 is not deployed).

PyPI · Transparency log: SHA-256 · ECDSA (partly PQ-safe). Rekor: entries hash-chained in a SHA-256 Merkle tree (post-quantum safe); checkpoints signed with ECDSA P-256 (rekor.sigstore.dev) or Ed25519 (Rekor v2 shards). A CRQC could sign a forked checkpoint, but not rewrite history a verifier already holds a checkpoint for.
PyPI · Transport (TLS): X25519MLKEM768 (partly PQ-safe). pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org and upload.pypi.org negotiate hybrid ML-KEM; certificates RSA-2048.

PyPI · Publish credential: OIDC RS256 (quantum-vulnerable). Trusted publishing trades a CI-issued OIDC token for a short-lived upload token. GitHub's and GitLab's OIDC tokens are RS256: a CRQC could forge one from the published JWKS and publish as any project. Long-lived API tokens are random secrets, which only harvested traffic would expose. PyPI's tokens are macaroons (HMAC-SHA256).
PyPI · MFA: TOTP · WebAuthn (partly PQ-safe). Mandatory. TOTP is symmetric; WebAuthn signatures are classical, with public keys known only to PyPI.
npm · Install hash: SHA-512 (PQ-safe). dist.integrity (SRI sha512), recorded in package-lock.json.

npm · Publisher signature: ECDSA P-256 (quantum-vulnerable). Optional provenance. Sigstore bundle: ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key, certified by Fulcio's ECDSA P-384 CA. A CRQC could forge the CA and mint certificates for any identity. A post-quantum (ML-DSA) Sigstore instance is targeted for mid-2027 as a separate, opt-in trust root.
npm · Registry signature: ECDSA P-256 (quantum-vulnerable). dist.signatures and the publish attestation are signed with npm's registry key (ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, published at /-/npm/v1/keys).

npm · Transparency log: SHA-256 · ECDSA (partly PQ-safe). Rekor: entries hash-chained in a SHA-256 Merkle tree (post-quantum safe); checkpoints signed with ECDSA P-256 (rekor.sigstore.dev) or Ed25519 (Rekor v2 shards). A CRQC could sign a forked checkpoint, but not rewrite history a verifier already holds a checkpoint for.

npm · Transport (TLS): TLS 1.2 · X25519 (quantum-vulnerable). registry.npmjs.org and api.npmjs.org refuse TLS 1.3 (protocol_version alert), so no hybrid key exchange is possible. Publish tokens sent today could be decrypted from recorded traffic later.

npm · Publish credential: OIDC RS256 (quantum-vulnerable). Trusted publishing trades a CI-issued OIDC token for a short-lived upload token. GitHub's and GitLab's OIDC tokens are RS256: a CRQC could forge one from the published JWKS and publish as any project. Long-lived API tokens are random secrets, which only harvested traffic would expose.

npm · MFA: TOTP · WebAuthn (partly PQ-safe). Security keys (WebAuthn) are the documented method and TOTP is being deprecated. TOTP is HMAC-SHA1 over a shared secret (post-quantum safe). Security keys sign with ECDSA/EdDSA, but their public keys are known only to the registry.
crates.io · Install hash: SHA-256 (PQ-safe). Cargo checks the index's cksum and records it in Cargo.lock.
crates.io · Publisher signature: none (not used). Nothing is signed.
crates.io · Registry signature: none (not used). The index is unsigned.
crates.io · Transparency log: none (not used). No log.
crates.io · Transport (TLS): X25519MLKEM768 (partly PQ-safe). crates.io, index.crates.io and static.crates.io negotiate hybrid ML-KEM; certificates RSA-2048.

crates.io · Publish credential: OIDC RS256 (quantum-vulnerable). Trusted publishing trades a CI-issued OIDC token for a short-lived upload token. GitHub's and GitLab's OIDC tokens are RS256: a CRQC could forge one from the published JWKS and publish as any project. Long-lived API tokens are random secrets, which only harvested traffic would expose.
crates.io · MFA: via GitHub (partly PQ-safe). Whatever the GitHub account uses: TOTP, WebAuthn/passkeys, GitHub Mobile or SMS.
RubyGems · Install hash: SHA-256 (PQ-safe). Compact-index checksums; Gemfile.lock CHECKSUMS since Bundler 2.6 (opt-in).

RubyGems · Publisher signature: ECDSA P-256 (quantum-vulnerable). Optional attestations. Sigstore bundle: ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key, certified by Fulcio's ECDSA P-384 CA. A CRQC could forge the CA and mint certificates for any identity. A post-quantum (ML-DSA) Sigstore instance is targeted for mid-2027 as a separate, opt-in trust root. Legacy gem cert signatures are RSA.
RubyGems · Registry signature: none (not used). rubygems.org signs nothing.

RubyGems · Transparency log: SHA-256 · ECDSA (partly PQ-safe). Rekor: entries hash-chained in a SHA-256 Merkle tree (post-quantum safe); checkpoints signed with ECDSA P-256 (rekor.sigstore.dev) or Ed25519 (Rekor v2 shards). A CRQC could sign a forked checkpoint, but not rewrite history a verifier already holds a checkpoint for.
RubyGems · Transport (TLS): X25519MLKEM768 (partly PQ-safe). rubygems.org and index.rubygems.org negotiate hybrid ML-KEM; certificates RSA-2048.

RubyGems · Publish credential: OIDC RS256 (quantum-vulnerable). Trusted publishing trades a CI-issued OIDC token for a short-lived upload token. GitHub's and GitLab's OIDC tokens are RS256: a CRQC could forge one from the published JWKS and publish as any project. Long-lived API tokens are random secrets, which only harvested traffic would expose.
RubyGems · MFA: TOTP · WebAuthn (partly PQ-safe). TOTP is symmetric; WebAuthn signatures are classical, with public keys known only to rubygems.org.
Go · Install hash: SHA-256 (PQ-safe). go.sum h1: hashes (SHA-256 over a file-hash list), checked against the checksum database.
Go · Publisher signature: none (not used). Module authors cannot sign.
Go · Registry signature: Ed25519 (quantum-vulnerable). sum.golang.org signs its tree heads as signed notes with Ed25519 (algorithm byte 0x01 in its key).

Go · Transparency log: SHA-256 · Ed25519 (partly PQ-safe). sum.golang.org: SHA-256 Merkle tree (post-quantum safe) with Ed25519-signed tree heads. go.sum then pins the hash itself, so a module already in go.sum stays protected.
Go · Transport (TLS): X25519MLKEM768 (partly PQ-safe). proxy.golang.org and sum.golang.org negotiate hybrid ML-KEM; certificates ECDSA P-256.

Go · Publish credential: forge SSH key (quantum-vulnerable). Releases are VCS tags, so publishing is a push to the forge: SSH keys (Ed25519/RSA, whose public halves are listed at github.com/{user}.keys) or HTTPS tokens. A CRQC could derive SSH private keys from those public keys.
Go · MFA: n/a (not used). No publisher accounts; the forge's own 2FA applies.

Maven Central · Install hash: SHA-1 / MD5 (weak already). Central serves .sha1 and .md5 for every file (.sha256/.sha512 optional); Maven 3 checks SHA-1 and only warns on mismatch. SHA-1 collisions are practical today.

Maven Central · Publisher signature: PGP RSA/EdDSA (quantum-vulnerable). Mandatory PGP. Latest releases of the 50 sampled artifacts: RSA 34, EdDSA 6, ECDSA 5, DSA 4, 1 unsigned (2006). Long-lived keys on public keyservers, so a CRQC could sign as any of them. RFC 9980 (2026-06) adds ML-DSA composites to OpenPGP, but GnuPG cannot sign with them yet and no sampled signature uses them. Optional Sigstore bundles as above.
Maven Central · Registry signature: none (not used). Central signs nothing itself.

Maven Central · Transparency log: SHA-256 · ECDSA (partly PQ-safe). Only for the optional .sigstore.json bundles. Rekor: entries hash-chained in a SHA-256 Merkle tree (post-quantum safe); checkpoints signed with ECDSA P-256 (rekor.sigstore.dev) or Ed25519 (Rekor v2 shards). A CRQC could sign a forked checkpoint, but not rewrite history a verifier already holds a checkpoint for.
Maven Central · Transport (TLS): X25519MLKEM768 (partly PQ-safe). repo1.maven.org, repo.maven.apache.org and central.sonatype.com negotiate hybrid ML-KEM; certificates ECDSA P-256.

Maven Central · Publish credential: bearer token (PQ-safe). Portal user tokens are random secrets; no OIDC path exists. Only harvested traffic could expose them, and the Central hosts already use hybrid key exchange.
Maven Central · MFA: TOTP (optional) (PQ-safe). Authenticator apps only (TOTP or Auth0 Guardian push); no security keys.
Packagist · Install hash: git SHA-1 (weak already). dist.shasum is empty for forge archives; the only pin is the commit id, a SHA-1 (GitHub detects known collision attacks, but the hash is SHA-1).
Packagist · Publisher signature: none (not used). Nothing is signed.
Packagist · Registry signature: none (not used). Packagist signs nothing.
Packagist · Transparency log: none (not used). The security-event log is not a log of artifacts.

Packagist · Transport (TLS): mixed (partly PQ-safe). packagist.org and repo.packagist.org negotiate hybrid ML-KEM, but archives come from GitHub (api.github.com, codeload.github.com), which offers only classical X25519.

Packagist · Publish credential: forge SSH key (quantum-vulnerable). Releases are VCS tags, so publishing is a push to the forge: SSH keys (Ed25519/RSA, whose public halves are listed at github.com/{user}.keys) or HTTPS tokens. A CRQC could derive SSH private keys from those public keys.
Packagist · MFA: TOTP (optional) (PQ-safe). TOTP only, optional.

svg.text: Hashes and symmetric secrets keep half their strength against a quantum computer (Grover); RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA are broken (Shor).
Hybrid TLS (X25519MLKEM768) protects recorded traffic, not server authentication: every certificate is still RSA or ECDSA. Hover a cell for details.
